idiom_name: serde derive on the message struct + impl From<&Order>/TryFrom<OrderMessage>
implementation_notes: The message is a dedicated struct with #[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)] and serde attributes (rename, default, deny_unknown_fields) declaring the wire policy, while the domain half uses the standard conversion traits - impl From<&Order> for OrderMessage and impl TryFrom<OrderMessage> for Order, with a resolver supplying referenced aggregates - so .into()/try_into() is the call site and the compiler refuses a mapping that forgot a field. What replaces the mapper class is the derived Serialize impl plus those conversion impls in one module; serde never touches the domain type, and serde_json/rmp-serde/prost's codec is chosen at the endpoint.
pitfalls: serde is permissive by default (unknown fields ignored, missing fields error only with default absent): state deny_unknown_fields/default per contract or a producer change becomes silent.
TryFrom that needs a repository to rehydrate references must not open a database connection inside the conversion; take the resolver as an argument of a mapper function instead.
Cloning ids and strings in From is the hot-path cost: map borrowed/Cow fields when messages are large and frequent.

variants.name: prost-generated .proto messages
variants.idiom_name: prost-generated message structs plus hand-written domain conversion
variants.implementation_notes: When the contract is a .proto, prost generates the message structs and the codec, so the mapper shrinks to OrderMessage::from(&order) plus impl TryFrom<OrderMessage> for Order - field numbers and reserved ranges replace hand-written version handling, and the generated type is the published contract. Choose it when several services share the schema or a schema registry already governs the channel, and keep the generated crate out of the domain's dependency graph.
pitfalls: prost generates plain fields with default values and no presence for scalars: absent-versus-zero must be decided in the mapper, not inferred from the default.
The generated code lives in its own crate and churns with every schema edit; version the schema and review generated diffs instead of letting them ride along in feature commits.
